name: The Client Gauntlet
purpose: People practise a difficult client conversation twice, with feedback in between, so the second attempt is better than the first.
audience: People who talk to clients, such as sales, consulting or account teams. 9 to 16 people, working in threes.
sequence: Watch a facilitator hold the conversation and say their thinking out loud
Agree a short checklist of what good looks like
Practise in threes: one speaks, one plays the client, one observes
Get feedback from the observer against the checklist
Hear the patterns the facilitators noticed
Practise again with a harder client
Write a plan for a real conversation coming up
methods: AI role-play; live actor; triad practice; video review
mechanics: Observation; deliberate practice; feedback; variability; transfer-appropriate practice
setup: Three practice rooms or stations; private replay spaces
needs: Two facilitators, or one facilitator and a subject expert who can demonstrate. One room big enough for threes to spread out, or two small rooms. Scenario cards written from the group's real clients, observer sheets, a timer. An AI role-play tool is optional practice before the day. If you use one, use a tool the client has approved and keep real client names and data out of it.
outputs: Before/after performance evidence; personal practice plan; reusable scenario bank
bestUse: Sales, consulting, discovery, executive influence
cautions: Write scenarios from real situations the group meets, not generic ones. Tell people at the start that nobody will be made to perform in front of the whole group.
plainName: Client conversation practice, half day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Say the aim and agree how feedback will be given: on what was said and done, not on the person.
Demonstration. One facilitator plays the consultant, the other plays the client. Pause three or four times to say what you are thinking and why.
The group lists what they saw. Turn it into a checklist of five things good looks like.
Each person picks a scenario card and plans their opening two minutes alone.
Round 1 in threes. 8 minutes of conversation, 4 minutes of feedback, then swap roles. Three turns.
Share two patterns you heard across the room. Re-teach one skill briefly and show it again.
Round 2 in the same threes. The client card now adds a complication, such as a new decision maker or a cut budget. Three turns.
Participants. Facilitators coach one group each.
Harder client cards, observer sheets, timer
Optional. One volunteer pair replays a short section for the group. The facilitator pauses and asks the group what to try.
Each person writes a practice plan: one thing to keep, one thing to change, and the real conversation they will use it in.
Pairs tell each other their plan. Close.

name: The Live Challenge
purpose: Teams work on a real problem the client has not yet solved and present a tested idea to the person who owns it.
audience: A mixed group from different departments. 12 to 16 people in teams of four, or up to 40 with more facilitators.
sequence: The sponsor explains the problem and what a useful answer would look like
Teams read the existing evidence
Teams talk to the people affected
Teams get advice from an expert
Teams build a rough version of their idea
Teams test it with the people it is for
Teams present, and the sponsor decides what happens next
methods: Live case; field study; design sprint; studio critique
mechanics: Authenticity; generation; social learning; feedback; transfer
setup: Team studios; sponsor touchpoints; prototype materials
needs: A named sponsor who wants the answer and attends the start and the end. Access to real data and real users. One facilitator per two or three teams. A table per team, wall space, and simple making materials. Someone who will own the idea after the event.
outputs: Tested concept; decision memo; 30-day implementation experiment
bestUse: Innovation, transformation and capability academies
cautions: Only run this if the sponsor will act on the result. Agree before the event what is confidential, who decides, and what happens to the ideas afterwards.
plainName: Team project on a real business problem, 2 to 3 days

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. The sponsor explains the problem, what has been tried, and what a useful answer would look like. Teams of four ask questions.
Teams read the existing evidence. Each team lists what is known, what is assumed, and what they need to ask. Break at 11:00.
Teams. One facilitator per two or three teams.
Teams prepare their interviews. Agree five questions, who asks and who takes notes.
Teams talk to the people affected. Work in pairs. Each pair holds two or three conversations of 20 minutes.
Interview guide, notebooks, a booked list of people to meet
Break, then teams put their notes on the wall, sort them into themes and choose one need to work on.
Expert advice. Each team gets 15 minutes with an expert. While they wait, each person sketches three ideas alone.
Each team says in one minute the need it chose and its leading idea. Close at 17:00.
Teams build a rough version of the idea. Paper, cardboard, a mock screen or a script are all fine. Break at 10:45.
Teams test it with the people it is for. Three people per team, 15 minutes each. Watch and listen. Do not sell the idea.
Rough versions, test note sheet, booked users
Teams change the idea using what the tests showed. Write a one-page decision note: the idea, what the test showed, what it needs, and a 30-day test.
Presentations to the sponsor. Seven minutes per team and five minutes of questions.
The sponsor says what happens next for each idea and names who owns it. Each person writes one thing they will do. Finish at 16:00.

name: The Learning Residency
purpose: Experienced people spend several days making real work, getting expert feedback and revising it.
audience: Experienced practitioners, such as designers, strategists or writers. 8 to 16 people per expert.
sequence: An expert teaches a short masterclass
The expert shows how they do the work
Long protected time to make your own work
The expert visits each person for feedback
Conversation over dinner
Quiet time alone to think
Revise the work the next day
Show the finished work on the wall
methods: Residency; studio; masterclass; critique; reflection
mechanics: Cognitive apprenticeship; feedback; identity; consolidation; social accountability
setup: Dedicated studio left intact overnight; exhibition wall
needs: One or two experts who can both show the work and give feedback on it. A room people can leave set up overnight. Wall space for the final display. An evening plan is optional.
outputs: Portfolio artefacts; revised work; community rituals; long-term craft goal
bestUse: Design, strategy, storytelling and leadership craft
cautions: Do not fill the timetable. The value is in long stretches of making, access to the expert, and a second attempt.
plainName: Craft retreat with expert feedback, 2 to 4 days

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Each person shows the work they have brought and says in two minutes what they want to improve.
Work in progress, wall or table space
Masterclass. The expert teaches one idea for 30 minutes, then does a piece of the work live and says their thinking out loud.
Screen or flipchart, the expert's own materials
Making time. Everyone works alone on their own piece. No teaching.
Making time continues. The expert visits each person for 10 minutes. With two experts, make it 20. Take a break when you need one.
Expert. Facilitator keeps the visiting order.
Pairs show each other where they have got to and say what they will change tomorrow. Leave the work out overnight. Free time from 17:30.
Dinner. Optional. Put one question on each table about the craft. The expert joins.
Quiet time alone. Walk or sit for 30 minutes without a phone. Write down what you will revise.
Revise the work. The expert makes a second visit to anyone who signs up.
Finish the work and put it on the wall with the first version beside it.
Wall show. The group walks round. Each person says in two minutes what changed and why. The expert gives each person one comment.
Each person writes one craft goal for the next three months and tells a partner. Close. Finish at 15:45.

name: The Failure Lab
purpose: Teams attempt a hard problem before they are taught the method, so the teaching answers questions they now have.
audience: Mixed experience. 8 to 16 people in teams of three or four.
sequence: Explain that the first attempt is meant to be hard
Teams attempt the problem with no teaching
Teams put their work on the wall and read each other's
The whole group discusses where the attempts went wrong, without blame
Teach the method, using the errors on the wall
Teams rework their approach
Teams attempt a second, similar problem
Compare the first and second attempts
methods: Productive failure; error analysis; contrast cases; retry
mechanics: Generation; productive failure; feedback; metacognition; contrast
setup: Team tables; visible work wall; private data capture
needs: One facilitator who knows the subject well enough to teach from the group's errors. A problem you have tested, that people can start on but will not solve well. A worked answer. Tables for teams, wall space, flipchart paper and sticky notes.
outputs: Failure patterns; revised strategy; before/after work sample
bestUse: Problem framing, innovation, systems and decision quality
cautions: This approach is called productive failure. It only works if the teaching follows straight after the attempt and the errors are treated as normal. Never single anyone out.
plainName: Try first, then teach, half day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Explain the plan. You will try a problem before being taught. Most first attempts will fall short and that is the point.
First attempt in teams of three or four. Give no hints on the method. Answer questions about the task only.
Teams post their work. Everyone walks round in silence and adds sticky notes: one thing that is clear, one question.
Whole-group discussion. Ask which approaches people tried and where they got stuck. Group the common errors on a flipchart with no team names.
Teach the method. Work through one example and point to the errors on the wall as you go.
Teams decide what they will do differently.
Second attempt on a new problem of the same type.
Teams put first and second attempts side by side and name the biggest difference.
Each person writes one thing they will do differently at work. Close.

name: The Future Simulation
purpose: Leadership teams make strategic decisions inside two or three different versions of the future and see which choices hold up in all of them.
audience: Leaders and strategy teams. 12 to 16 people in two or three teams, or up to 48 with a larger delivery team.
sequence: Read a wall of trends and early signs of change
Each team is given one version of the future
People take roles
Teams make decisions against the clock
The facilitators add surprise events
Teams see how their choices affect the other teams
A challenge group argues against each plan
Test the current strategy against every version of the future
Discuss what was learned
methods: Scenario planning; business simulation; role-play; red teaming
mechanics: Narrative; variability; emotion regulation; reflection; transfer
setup: Separate scenario rooms or zones; central mission control
needs: Someone to write the versions of the future in advance. Two people to run the exercise and issue the surprise events. A simple set of rules for what each decision leads to. A zone or room per team and one central table for the people running it.
outputs: No-regret moves; signposts; decision principles; risk log
bestUse: Strategy, AI disruption, resilience and operating-model change
cautions: These are stories about what could happen, not predictions. Keep the detail short so people argue about decisions, not about the story.
plainName: Strategy rehearsal across possible futures, one day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Say the aim. Say plainly that the versions of the future are stories about what could happen, not predictions.
Trends wall. Pairs walk the wall and put dots on the three signs of change that matter most to the business.
Trend cards on the wall, sticky dots
Two or three teams of four to six. Each team gets one version of the future on one page. Read it, then take roles such as chief executive, finance, operations and customer.
Round 1. Each team makes three decisions in 30 minutes and hands in a decision sheet. The central table works out the results from the rules and hands them back.
Both facilitators at the central table
Round 2. Each team gets a surprise event card. They decide again in 25 minutes. Results come back.
Teams tell the room what they chose and what happened. The facilitators show how each team's choices affected the others.
Challenge group. Two people from each team move to another team and argue against its plan for 15 minutes. The team answers and adjusts.
Mixed groups take the current strategy. For each part, mark on a grid whether it holds, bends or breaks in each version of the future.
Current strategy on one page, grid on flipchart
Whole group. List the moves that hold up in every version, the early signs to watch for, and the risks.
Each person writes one decision they would now make differently and tells a neighbour. Close.

name: The Skill Arcade
purpose: People move round a set of short practice stations, each on one small skill, and leave knowing which skills they still need to work on.
audience: 20 to 80 people. For 8 to 16, run three or four stations in one room.
sequence: A short self-check to see where each person starts
Everyone gets a card listing the stations
20 minute stations in rotation
A challenge card at each station
A drop-in table for expert help
A check at the end against a set standard
Each person chooses a follow-up exercise
methods: Learning stations; drills; clinics; mastery checks
mechanics: Deliberate practice; interleaving; feedback; autonomy; mastery
setup: 5–10 clearly branded stations; central orientation and recovery area
needs: One facilitator per station of 6 to 10 people. The same marking checklist at every station. Someone to keep time and move people on. Clear signs and a place to sit out.
outputs: Individual skill profile; completed challenge cards; follow-up drill prescription
bestUse: Large cohorts needing active practice without plenary monotony
cautions: Moving between stations takes longer than you think, so allow five minutes each time. Use the same standard at every station.
plainName: Rotating skill stations, half or full day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome for up to 40 people. Explain how the stations work and introduce the timekeeper. Say where the drop-in table and the sitting-out area are.
Signs, floor plan on a slide or flipchart
Self-check. Each person rates themselves on each skill on their station card, alone. Split into four groups of up to 10 by card colour.
Station cards in four colours, pens
Station round 1. Five minutes of demonstration, 12 minutes of practice in pairs on the challenge card, three minutes of marking against the checklist. Then five minutes to move.
Station facilitators. Timekeeper rings a bell.
Station round 2. Same pattern, then five minutes to move.
Break. The drop-in table is open for anyone who wants help with a skill.
Station round 3. Same pattern, then five minutes to move.
Station round 4. Same pattern, then five minutes to move back to the main area.
End check. Each person goes to the station for their weakest skill and does one short task. The facilitator marks it against the checklist.
Each person picks a follow-up exercise from the list, writes when they will do it and tells a partner. Close.

name: The Field Expedition
purpose: The group visits a real workplace or service, records what they see, and turns it into ideas to test.
audience: Innovation, operations or leadership groups. 10 to 16 people per facilitator, up to 30.
sequence: Teach people how to observe and take notes
Visit the site, or use a service as a customer would
Record what you see and hear
Talk to the people who work there or use it
Back in the room, sort the notes into themes
Map the opportunities
Each person commits to one next step
methods: Field study; learning walk; ethnographic observation; studio synthesis
mechanics: Situated learning; attention; curiosity; reflection; transfer
setup: Real site plus a nearby synthesis space
needs: Permission from the site and from the people being observed. An observation sheet. Transport and a host at the site. A room nearby for the afternoon. A plan for anyone who cannot do the visit on foot.
outputs: Evidence wall; insights; opportunity backlog; questions for experimentation
bestUse: Customer experience, systems, service and operational learning
cautions: The people you visit are hosts, not exhibits. Get consent, keep what you hear confidential, and remind the group that one visit is one day's evidence.
plainName: Site visit and analysis day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome in the room near the site. Say the aim and the rules: the people you visit are hosts, what you hear stays confidential, no photos without permission.
Teach observing. Write down what you see and hear, not what you think it means. Pairs practise for five minutes on the room around them and compare notes.
Give each pair one thing to watch for. Travel to the site. The host welcomes the group and says where you can and cannot go.
Lead facilitator, then the site host
Observe in pairs for 45 minutes. Stay out of the way. Anyone who cannot do the visit on foot follows the seated or remote plan.
Talk to people who work there or use the service. Each pair holds two conversations of 15 minutes.
Thank the host. Travel back. Lunch.
Each pair copies its strongest notes onto sticky notes, one observation per note.
Groups of four to six sort the notes into themes on the wall and name each theme.
Map the opportunities. For each theme, write what could be improved and place it on a grid of value against effort. Mark anything that rests on a single observation.
Whole group chooses three to five opportunities to test and writes the question each test would answer.
Each person writes one next step and says it aloud. Agree what you will send the host. Close.

name: The Capability Launch
purpose: A group builds a skill over 90 days, starting with a residential and continuing with a work project, peer groups and manager check-ins.
audience: People in the same role or department. 12 to 16 per group, or up to 100 run as several groups.
sequence: A skills check before the start
A residential of two or three days
Each person sets a personal plan
A project at work that uses the skill
Small peer groups that meet regularly
Check-ins with each person's manager
Short refreshers spaced over the weeks
People show what they can do at 30, 60 and 90 days
duration: 90 days, starting with a residential of 2 to 3 days
methods: Cohort; simulation; project; coaching; spacing; portfolio
mechanics: Spacing; social accountability; mastery; implementation intentions; transfer
setup: Retreat venue plus digital cohort hub and scheduled follow-ups
needs: One person who owns the whole programme. Managers who have agreed to their part. Coaches. A checklist for judging the work. A venue for the residential and an online space for the group.
outputs: Verified workplace outcomes; portfolio; capability data; continuing community
bestUse: AI, leadership, sales or role academies
cautions: Get managers and work projects agreed before you launch. Measure what people do at work, not only attendance and feedback scores.
plainName: Three-month skills programme with a residential start

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Skills check. Each person does a short practical task and rates themselves. Each manager has a 30 minute call to agree their part and a work project.
Skills check task, judging checklist, manager briefing note
Residential starts. Welcome. Explain the 90 days. Show the pattern from the skills check without naming anyone.
Coaches demonstrate the skill. The group goes through the checklist. Break at 11:00. Then a first practice in threes with one person observing.
Second practice on a harder case. Coaches give feedback against the checklist. Break at 15:00.
Coaches. One coach per 6 to 8 people.
Form peer groups of four. Each group agrees when and how it will meet. Close at 17:00. Dinner is optional.
Pairs write down from memory what they learned yesterday. Then a third practice on a case from their own work. Break at 11:00.
Each person defines their work project: what they will do, by when, and how they will show it worked. A coach checks each one.
Personal plan. Each person writes three lines in the form: when this happens, I will do this. The peer group tests each plan.
Peer groups book their first three meetings. Explain what people will show at 30, 60 and 90 days. Close. Finish at 15:30.
Manager check-in in week 1, then monthly, 30 minutes. Peer groups meet for 45 minutes every two weeks. A 10 minute refresher task goes out every two weeks.
Check-in prompts, refresher tasks, online group space
Each person shows a piece of real work to their peer group and a coach online, 90 minutes. The coach judges it against the checklist.
Final showing, half a day, managers invited. Each person presents what they did at work. Agree how the peer groups carry on.
Judging checklist, record of each person's work

name: The Executive Decision Room
purpose: Senior leaders decide on a realistic case alone, then as a group, then again after being challenged, and see what changed their minds.
audience: Senior leaders. 8 to 16 people.
sequence: Hand out the case
Each person writes their own decision and how sure they are
Small teams agree one decision
Each team's decision is argued against by another team
Everyone imagines the decision failed and lists why
Each person writes a revised decision
Discuss who changed their mind and why
methods: Decision-forcing case; fishbowl; red team; premortem
mechanics: Generation; calibration; social learning; cognitive conflict; feedforward
setup: Boardroom layout with visible evidence and decision log
needs: One facilitator who is not part of the leadership team. A case close to the decisions this team makes, on two or three pages. A sponsor who takes part as an equal. A boardroom or horseshoe layout, flipcharts and decision cards.
outputs: Decision rationale; assumptions; risk mitigations; challenge norms
bestUse: Strategy, investments, governance and transformation decisions
cautions: Senior voices can silence others. Always collect each person's decision in writing before any discussion, and ask the most senior person to speak last.
plainName: Decision-making practice for a leadership team, half day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Say the purpose and the rules for challenge: argue with the reasoning, not the person, and the most senior person speaks last.
Hand out the case. Everyone reads alone.
Printed case, two to three pages
Each person writes their decision, their main reason, and how sure they are from 0 to 100 per cent.
Show the spread of decisions and confidence on a flipchart with no names. Do not discuss yet.
Teams of four agree one decision and their three strongest reasons.
Challenge round. Each team presents for 5 minutes. Another team then has 10 minutes to find the weak points.
Imagine it is a year on and the decision failed. Everyone lists reasons alone for 5 minutes, then the group pools them.
Each person writes a revised decision and confidence level.
Discuss who changed their mind and what changed it. Then discuss what made challenge easy or hard in this room.
First and second cards side by side
The group agrees three rules for challenge in their real meetings. The sponsor closes.

name: The Unconference Studio
purpose: Participants set the agenda and run the sessions themselves, and the day ends with shared conclusions and named owners.
audience: An experienced group from mixed roles who already share some background. 30 to 120 people.
sequence: Everyone reads the same short briefing
People propose sessions and build the timetable on a wall
Participants run their sessions
Experts walk between sessions
Each session posts its notes for everyone to read
Small groups pull the notes into conclusions
People sign up to carry things on
methods: Open Space; peer teaching; studio work; gallery critique
mechanics: Autonomy; social learning; generation; identity; accountability
setup: Large marketplace plus multiple breakout studios and exhibition space
needs: One clear question for the day. A one-page sheet for each session to record its notes. A note-taker per session. One large room for the timetable wall and several smaller spaces. Two facilitators for the final pulling-together.
outputs: Community-owned playbook; prototypes; named practice groups
bestUse: Communities of practice and capability festivals
cautions: This format is based on Open Space. Run it only with people who already know the basics, and protect the last hour for conclusions and owners.
plainName: Participant-led conference day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome in one big circle. State the question for the day. Explain the rules: anyone can propose a session, and if you are not learning or contributing, move to another one.
The question on a large sign
Everyone reads the same short briefing in silence for 10 minutes, then talks about it in threes.
People propose sessions. Write a title and your name on a sheet, say it to the room in one sentence, and stick it on the timetable wall.
Lead facilitator. Second facilitator runs the wall.
Timetable wall with a grid of times and spaces, sheets, markers, tape
Break. Merge sessions that overlap. People read the wall and choose.
Session round 1, 45 minutes. The person who proposed it runs it. A note-taker fills in the one-page sheet. Experts walk between sessions.
Note sheets, flipchart in each space
Note-takers post their sheets on the notes wall. Everyone moves.
Lunch. The notes wall stays open.
Session round 3, 45 minutes. Same pattern. Post notes at the end.
Break. Everyone reads the notes wall and puts dots on the notes that matter most.
Pulling together. Groups of six to eight each take one cluster of notes and write three conclusions and one thing still unresolved.
Each group reports in two minutes. With more than 10 groups, post the sheets and hear only the top conclusion from each.
Sign-up. Put up one sheet for each conclusion that needs work. People sign as owner or helper. Each owner writes a first date.
Closing circle. Say who will write up the notes and by when. Finish at 16:30.

name: The Simulation Ladder
purpose: People practise a skill in simple scenarios first, then in more realistic ones, ending with a full scenario.
audience: People new to the skill or with some experience. 12 to 16 with two facilitators, up to 30 with more.
sequence: Watch a demonstration
Try a simple scenario
Repeat it with coaching
Try a different scenario
Practise with an actor or a trained colleague playing the other person
Do a full scenario from start to finish
Review it later, once people have had time to think
methods: Worked example; low/high-fidelity simulation; role-play; coaching
mechanics: Scaffolding; fading; deliberate practice; variability; delayed feedback
setup: Practice rooms of increasing realism; observation area
needs: Scenario briefs that get harder in steps. Facilitators or actors to play the other person. One checklist of what good looks like, used at every step. Small rooms or corners for practice.
outputs: Competency profile; recorded capstone; targeted follow-up plan
bestUse: Interpersonal, operational and safety-critical capability
cautions: More realistic is not always better. Add realism only when it adds something people will meet in the real job.
plainName: Role-play practice that gets more realistic in steps, 1 to 2 days

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Say the aim and agree how feedback will be given. Nobody will be made to perform in front of the whole group.
Demonstration. The two facilitators play the scenario. The group lists what they saw and compares it with the checklist.
Checklist of what good looks like
Step 1. A simple scenario in threes: one speaks, one plays the other person, one observes. Six minutes, three minutes of feedback, then swap. Three turns.
Simple scenario briefs, observer sheets, timer
Step 2. The same scenario again with coaching. A facilitator stops each person once, suggests one change, and they go again.
Step 3. A different scenario that uses the same skill. New threes. Three turns.
The facilitators share two patterns they heard and show one skill again.

Step 4. Two groups of up to eight, each with an actor or trained colleague. Each person has eight minutes with the actor and four of feedback. The rest observe with the checklist. Short break halfway.
Actors or facilitators play the other person
Step 5. The full scenario from start to finish in threes, 12 minutes each. Observers fill in the checklist but keep it back for now.
Each person writes their own review first. Then observers hand over their sheets and the three talk it through.
Each person writes a follow-up plan and tells a partner. Close. Finish at 16:45.
A 30 minute call in the same threes. Each person says what they have tried since and what they would now do differently in the full scenario.
Participants. One facilitator joins each call if possible.

name: The Mastery Circuit
purpose: Everyone works towards the same practical standard, with extra help and a second assessment for those who need it.
audience: People with mixed starting levels. 12 to 16 with two facilitators, up to 60 with more assessors.
sequence: A test at the start to see who needs what
Short teaching sessions on the gaps
Practice stations
An assessment against the standard
Extra help for anyone who did not pass
A second assessment
A harder task for those who passed early
methods: Diagnostic; mastery learning; clinics; stations; reassessment
mechanics: Mastery; feedback; retrieval; autonomy; scaffolding
setup: Multiple routes with clear signage; assessment and remediation zones
needs: A written standard that describes what a pass looks like. Assessors who have marked sample work together so they agree. Enough coaches and enough time for second attempts.
outputs: Verified mastery record; individual gap report; extension challenge
bestUse: Technical, regulatory and prerequisite skills
cautions: Do not run this unless you have time and staff for second assessments. Assess people doing the task, not only a quiz.
plainName: Practice and re-test until everyone reaches the standard, 1 to 2 days

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Work beforehand. Each person reads or watches the materials and tries the self-check. Assessors mark sample work together until they agree.
Materials, self-check, written standard, sample work
Welcome. Show the written standard and an example of a pass. Say that second attempts are a normal part of the day.
Start test. Each person does a short practical task alone for 20 minutes. The facilitators mark it against the standard and give each person a sheet showing their gaps.
Break. The facilitators finish marking and sort people into teaching sessions.
Short teaching sessions on the gaps. Two run side by side, 20 minutes each, then repeat. People go to the ones they need. Anyone with no gaps starts the practice stations.
Practice stations. Three stations, each on one part of the task. Work in pairs, 20 minutes per station, and mark your own work against the standard.
First assessment. Each person does the full task while an assessor watches, about 10 minutes each. Those waiting keep practising at the stations.
Assessment task, marking sheets, timetable of slots
Break. Each person gets their result in private, with what to fix.
Extra help in a small group for anyone who did not pass, on their specific gaps. Those who passed start a harder task in pairs.
One facilitator coaches. One sets up the harder task.
Second assessment for those who need it. Same standard, different example of the task. The others finish the harder task.
One facilitator assesses. One supports the harder task.
Each person gets their record. Anyone not yet at the standard agrees a date for another attempt. Everyone writes one thing to keep practising. Close.

name: The Challenge Tournament
purpose: A large group produces many ideas, then narrows them in rounds against agreed criteria, and the best get money for a small test.
audience: An innovation group. 30 to 150 people.
sequence: Explain the challenge
Fast rounds of idea generation
Teams add evidence to each idea
People walk round and review each other's ideas
Agree the selection criteria and practise using them
Narrow the ideas in rounds
Teams get expert advice
Final pitches, and funding for tests
methods: Innovation tournament; pitch; peer marketplace; prototype
mechanics: Generation; contrast; social learning; feedback; reinforcement
setup: Large plenary, team bays, visible tournament board
needs: Selection criteria published before the day. Judges from different backgrounds. A small budget for tests. A large room, team areas and a board showing progress.
outputs: Prioritised portfolio; experiment charters; evidence gaps
bestUse: Innovation portfolios, sustainability and process improvement
cautions: Competitions can reward confident presenters and familiar ideas. Score the idea separately from the pitch, and fund tests, not winners.
plainName: Ideas competition with staged selection, one day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. The sponsor explains the challenge, the test budget and the selection criteria. Say that the money funds tests, not winners. Sit in teams of five or six.
Challenge brief, criteria on the wall, progress board
Idea rounds. Three rounds of 10 minutes, each with a different prompt. Write alone for five minutes, one idea per card, then share and build at the table.
Each team picks its two strongest ideas and writes each on an idea sheet. Break at 10:45.
Table facilitators, one per four or five teams
Practise the criteria. Everyone scores the same two sample ideas, compares scores at the table, and the facilitator settles the differences.
Teams add evidence to each idea sheet: who it helps, what is known, and what is assumed.
Lunch. Idea sheets go up on the wall.
Walk round. Everyone reads the sheets and scores ideas against the criteria. You cannot score your own. No pitching. The sheets speak for themselves.
Round 1 result. Scores go up on the board and about a third of the ideas go forward. People whose ideas dropped out join a team that is still in.
Expert advice. Experts spend 10 minutes with each team. Teams design a small test: what they will try, what it costs, and what result would change their mind.
Break. Judges read the updated idea sheets and test plans.
Round 2. Judges score the written sheets against the criteria. The top six go to the final. Teams prepare a four minute pitch.
Final pitches. Four minutes each and three minutes of questions. Judges score the idea and the pitch separately. Only the idea score counts.
Lead facilitator keeps time. Judges score.
Judges confer for 10 minutes while each team lists what evidence is still missing. Announce which tests get money, who owns each, and the date to report back. Finish at 17:00.
Follow-up. Test owners report what they found in a one hour meeting. The sponsor decides what continues.

What happens
Who leads
Materials

Ten minute sessions in threes. One runs the session, two take part. Five minutes of feedback against the checklist, then swap.
Demonstration of handling difficult behaviour: someone who talks over others, someone silent, someone who challenges. The group starts a list of responses.

Share patterns and add to the response list. Brief for tomorrow: prepare a 20 minute session this evening. Close at 16:00.

Both facilitators, one coaching each group
Final preparation for the 20 minute sessions. Lunch at 12:30.

Participants. Each facilitator moves between two groups.

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials

Screen, approved AI tool, tested prompts

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. State the problem in one sentence. Say that the map is a simplified picture and will have gaps.

Build the map. Groups of four write the parts of the problem on cards: people, teams, steps, and things that pile up. Then the whole group places them on the wall and draws arrows for what affects what.
Large wall or floor, cards, tape, markers
Check against the evidence. Pairs take a section each, compare it with the data, and mark each link green for evidence, amber for believed and red for a guess.
Roles. Each person takes the role of a group involved, not their own. Stand by that group's place on the map and say what it wants and what gets in its way.

Change cards in a different colour

Mapping facilitator. Second facilitator keeps the log.

Groups of four each design one small test: what changes, where, for how long, what to measure, and who owns it.
Read out the tests. Name who keeps the map and the assumptions log. Close.

name: The Crisis Command Exercise

Announce the incident
People take up their crisis roles
Decisions against the clock
New events arrive, such as a press call or a customer complaint
Updates show the effect of earlier decisions
Hand over to a second shift
Review straight afterwards
Review again later, once people have had time to think

bestUse: Cyber, business continuity, reputational and client crises

What happens
Who leads
Materials

Role cards, observer sheets, name badges for roles

Helper 1 feeds in events. Helper 2 keeps the log. Shift B responds.
Second set of event cards, observer sheets for shift A
End the exercise. Everyone steps out of role and takes two minutes alone to write what stood out.
Review. Walk through the log in order. For each decision point ask what the plan said, what happened and what was missing. Keep it on the plan and the process, not on people.
Facilitator, with observers adding what they saw
List the gaps in roles and in the written plan. Give each an owner. Set the date for the second review in one to two weeks.
Facilitator and the team's most senior person
Finish. The facilitator stays for anyone who wants to talk.

name: The Leadership Mirror

Review the recording or the notes

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials

Each person writes the leadership challenge they are working on and predicts how they will behave in the task. They read both to their group.

Each person reads their notes alone and chooses one change to test in the afternoon.

Coaches feed back on the one change only, 5 minutes each. The group adds what they noticed.

One sentence each to the whole group. Close. Finish at 16:30.

Groups list what the team has been assuming. They pick three assumptions to check and write interview questions for them.

Customer conversations. Each group talks to one customer for 30 minutes, in person or by video call. If no customers are available, use an actor briefed from real cases and say so. One person asks, one takes notes, the rest listen.
Interview rooms or video calls, consent forms, note sheets
Groups report what they heard and update the wall. Keep three things apart: what was observed, what the team thinks it means, and what the team is guessing.
Each group builds one rough improvement, such as a redrawn form, a new script or a mocked-up screen. Each writes down what they expect customers to do with it.
Paper, card, pens, tape, laptops if needed
Quick tests. Each group shows its improvement to two customers, 15 minutes each, and watches what they do before asking anything.
Groups. Second facilitator runs the customer timetable.
Interview rooms or video calls, test note sheet
Groups compare what happened with what they expected, and change the improvement or drop it.
Each group states its tested improvement, what is still a guess, and who takes it forward. Close.

name: The Negotiation Dojo
purpose: People practise negotiating in short rounds, get feedback, and try again under changed conditions.
audience: Leaders, salespeople and delivery teams. 9 to 16 people, working in threes.
sequence: Teach a small set of negotiation principles
Short drills on single skills
A paired negotiation with an observer
Feedback from the observer
Change one condition
Negotiate again
Review what the observers wrote
A final negotiation between three teams
methods: Role-play; deliberate practice; simulation; coaching
mechanics: Practice; variability; feedback; emotional regulation; calibration
setup: Multiple small rooms; timers; private preparation space
needs: One facilitator with negotiation experience. A second helps above 12 people. Briefs that give each side something to trade. Observer sheets, timers, and space for threes to work apart.
outputs: Negotiation strategy; personal tendencies; tested alternative moves
bestUse: Commercial, stakeholder and internal negotiation
cautions: Being aggressive is not the same as being skilled. Say clearly in the briefs who holds more power, and that lying is out of bounds.
plainName: Negotiation practice day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Each person writes down a real negotiation they have coming up.
Teach four ideas: what each side needs, not only what they ask for. Your fallback if there is no deal. Who makes the first offer. Trading, not giving things away.
Flipchart or slides, one worked example
Drills in pairs, five minutes each: asking why, making a first offer, responding to a flat no.
Round 1 in threes. Two negotiate, one observes. 10 minutes to prepare, 15 to negotiate, 10 for feedback.
Brief A for each side, observer sheets
Write every group's outcome on a flipchart. Discuss why the same brief produced different deals.
Round 2. Same brief with one condition changed, such as a closer deadline. Rotate roles.
Round 3. New brief, last rotation, so everyone has observed once.
Each person reads the observer sheets written about them and notes one habit. Then a 15 minute break.
Final negotiation between three teams with some shared and some competing aims. 20 minutes to prepare, 40 to negotiate.
Discuss the final negotiation: what each team wanted, what they got, and what moved the deal.
Each person plans their own real negotiation using the four ideas, then talks it through with a partner.

name: The Prototype Marketplace
purpose: Teams build rough versions of their ideas, test them on each other, and improve them in a second round.
audience: Design or innovation groups. 12 to 16 in four teams, up to 80.
sequence: Agree the problem
Build a rough version quickly
Set up a stall for each team
Testers visit each stall in rotation
Testers leave written feedback
Teams improve their idea
A second round of testing
Pull together what was learned
methods: Prototyping; gallery walk; peer marketplace; critique
mechanics: Generation; feedback; contrast; embodied cognition; social learning
setup: Large room with team stalls, prototype materials and feedback tokens
needs: A written question for each prototype to answer. Testers who are not on the team, ideally people the idea is for. Card, paper, tape and pens. A timekeeper. A large room with a table per team.
outputs: Multiple prototypes; test evidence; revised concept; reusable patterns
bestUse: Service, product, process and learning design
cautions: The most popular idea in the room is not proven to work. Make each team write down what their prototype is testing before the testers arrive.
plainName: Build, test and rebuild ideas, half or full day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Agree the problem. Form four teams of 3 or 4. Each team writes the one question its prototype will answer.
The problem on a flipchart, question cards
Build round 1. Teams make a rough version from card and paper. Give time checks at 20 and 35 minutes.
Card, paper, tape, pens, scissors, timer
Each team sets up a stall and puts its question card where testers can see it.
One table per team, question cards

Test round 1. One or two people stay to host each stall. Everyone else visits the other three stalls, 8 minutes each, and leaves a written feedback card before moving on. Outside testers join here if you have them.
Feedback cards, timer, a bell or chime
Teams read their feedback, decide what to change and rebuild.
Test round 2. Hosts and visitors swap, so everyone tests and everyone hosts. Same rotation.
Each team writes three lines: what we tested, what we learned, and what is still unproven.
Each team reports in 3 minutes. The facilitator lists what was learned across teams. Remind the group that a popular idea has not been shown to work.
Agree what happens to each idea next. Close. Finish at 13:00.

name: The Manager Transfer Lab
purpose: Each learner and their manager agree how the new skill will be used back at work and what the manager will do to help.
audience: Learners and their line managers, in pairs. 8 to 16 pairs.
sequence: The learner shows their manager what they can now do
The manager watches with a short guide
Together they list what could get in the way at work
They agree who does what
They write if-then plans for the likely obstacles
Managers practise a coaching conversation
The manager commits time or resources
They book a review in 30 days
duration: About 3.5 hours, best as the last session of a programme
methods: Transfer planning; coaching; implementation intentions; social accountability
mechanics: Implementation intentions; relevance; feedforward; habit and cue design
setup: Paired seating with private planning space
needs: A short briefing sent to managers a week ahead. A planning sheet for each pair. Seating in pairs with some privacy. Someone senior to take obstacles that a pair cannot fix themselves.
outputs: Manager–learner contract; protected practice time; review date; barrier plan
bestUse: Any programme where workplace conditions determine application
cautions: What a manager sees here is for development and must not go into appraisal. Many obstacles are about workload or process, so fix those and do not put it all on the learner.
plainName: Planning session for learners and their managers

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Say the aim. Say that what managers see today is for development and does not go into appraisal.
Learners set up what they will show. In another corner, managers are briefed on the watching guide: what to look for and what to ask afterwards.
Facilitator briefs managers. Learners prepare alone.
Watching guide, anything learners need to demonstrate
Demonstrations in clusters of four pairs. Each learner takes about 8 minutes to show their manager and the cluster one thing they can now do.
Watching guides, timer for each cluster
Each pair sits alone. The manager says what they saw. Together they list what could get in the way at work, such as workload, process or tools.
Pairs agree who does what. They write an if-then plan for each of the three most likely obstacles. They mark any obstacle they cannot fix themselves.
Managers move into threes and practise a 5-minute coaching conversation: one coaches, one plays a learner, one observes, then swap. Learners meet together and plan their first two weeks of practice.
Facilitator with managers. Learners work on their own.
Pairs bring the obstacles they cannot fix. The senior person answers each one: yes, no, or who will decide and by when.
Back in pairs. The manager writes down the time or resources they will give. Both sign the sheet and put the 30-day review in their diaries now.
Each pair says one commitment aloud. Close.

name: The Reflection Observatory
purpose: People take quiet time to work out what they have learned and decide what they will do differently.
audience: Any retreat group. 8 to 16 with one facilitator, up to 60.
sequence: Look back over the day's notes and work
Quiet time alone with written prompts
Write down one decision and what you expect to happen
Talk it through with a partner who only listens
Optional sharing with the group
Recall it from memory the next morning
duration: 75 minutes at the end of a day, plus 10 minutes the next morning
methods: Silent reflection; journalling; peer reflection; concept mapping
mechanics: Reflection; consolidation; calibration; implementation intentions; identity
setup: Quiet individual zones plus optional walking route and paired spaces
needs: One facilitator. Prompt cards and a notebook each. Quiet places to sit, and a walking route if the venue has one. An alternative for anyone who would rather talk or draw than write.
outputs: Revised mental model; decision journal; commitments; personal narrative
bestUse: Multi-day retreats and emotionally or cognitively intense programmes
cautions: Ask people to reflect on what happened, not on feelings in general, and to end with a decision. Nobody should be made to share.
plainName: Guided reflection session for a retreat

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Explain the session. What you write is private. Sharing at the end is optional.
Look back through your notes, the flipcharts and any work from the day. List three moments that mattered.
Quiet time alone, sitting or walking, with three prompts: what surprised me, what I now think differently, what I am still unsure about.
Write one decision you are making, what you expect to happen, and how you will know.
In pairs, one speaks for five minutes while the other only listens, then asks one question. Swap.
Optional sharing in a circle. One sentence each. Anyone can pass.
Close. Say that tomorrow starts with recall. Finish at 17:15.
For 10 minutes, write yesterday's decision and one idea from memory, then check against your notebook.

name: The Knowledge Expedition
purpose: A group reads a set of chosen sources on a new topic, teaches each other, and writes a short shared guide.
audience: Professionals learning a new field. 12 to 16 works well, up to 40.
sequence: Agree the questions to answer
Small groups read different sources
Groups teach each other what they found
Put the findings on a shared wall map
An expert questions the findings
Write up the conclusions
Produce a short guide
Teach it back to the whole group
methods: Research sprint; reciprocal teaching; concept mapping; teach-back
mechanics: Retrieval; elaboration; social learning; metacognition; dual coding
setup: Source library, research stations, large evidence map
needs: Sources chosen and checked in advance by someone who knows the field. An expert for the challenge session. A one-page sheet for summarising each source. Tables for reading groups and a large wall.
outputs: Evidence map; field guide; unanswered questions; source index
bestUse: AI, regulation, emerging technology and new market understanding
cautions: Check the quality of the sources before the day. On the wall, mark what the evidence shows separately from what people agree on, and make sure everyone sees the whole picture.
plainName: Group research sprint on a new topic, 1 to 2 days

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Agree the three or four questions the group wants answered and write them across the wall.
Reading. Groups of four each read a different set of sources. They fill in a one-page sheet for each source: what it says, how it knows, and how far to trust it.
Reading groups. Facilitator moves between them.
Teach each other. Form new groups with one person from each reading group. Each person has 8 minutes to teach what their sources said.
Wall map. Everyone posts findings under the questions. Use one colour for what the evidence shows and another for what the group agrees on. Mark the gaps.
Two colours of sticky note, pens
Expert challenge. The expert walks the wall, questions the findings and points out what is missing or overstated. The group corrects the map as they go.
Writing. Each group takes one question and writes half a page: what is known, what is not known, and what it means for our work.
Laptops or paper, a shared document
Put the guide together. Two volunteers edit the half pages into one short guide. The others build the source list and the list of open questions.
Teach back. Each group presents its question to the whole room in 6 minutes. The expert corrects anything that is wrong.
Each person writes one thing they will use and one thing they still need to find out. Agree who gets the guide and who keeps it up to date.

name: The Peer Consultancy
purpose: One person brings a real work problem and a small group helps them think it through by asking questions before giving any advice.
audience: Experienced leaders or practitioners. 8 to 16 people in circles of four to six.
sequence: One person describes their problem
The group asks questions to get the facts
Everyone thinks in silence
The group asks open questions to help the owner think
Each person offers one view and one option
The owner says what they heard and what they will try
Check back later on what happened
duration: 2.5 hours for two rounds. Check back three to four weeks later.
methods: Action learning; peer coaching; case clinic
mechanics: Social learning; self-explanation; feedforward; accountability; transfer
setup: Small circles; visible question protocol; no-slide rule
needs: One facilitator who knows the format. With two circles, brief a participant to keep time in the second. Chairs in circles, no tables, no slides. The steps on a flipchart. A date for the check-back.
outputs: Experiment plan for each owner; peer support network; evidence review
bestUse: Leadership, project and client-delivery challenges
cautions: This is based on action learning. Hold the group to questions before advice, and agree at the start that what is said stays in the room.
plainName: Peer problem-solving rounds

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Explain the format and three rules: what is said stays here, questions come before advice, no slides.
Everyone writes a real problem in three sentences. Each circle picks two to work on today.
Round 1. The owner describes the problem. No interruptions.
Questions to get the facts straight. No suggestions dressed up as questions.
Circle. Facilitator steps in if advice creeps in.
Three minutes of silence. Each person writes what they think is going on.
Open questions that help the owner think. Still no advice.
Each person offers one view of what might be happening and one option. The owner listens and takes notes without replying.
The owner says what struck them and the one thing they will try.
Round 2 with a new owner, same steps, 45 minutes.
Whole group. Discuss which questions helped most and why.
Each owner says what they will try and by when. Agree a date to check back. Finish at 12:00.

name: The Observatory and Control Room
purpose: A team practises spotting a problem in live figures, deciding what to do, and handing over to the next shift.
audience: Operations, product and service teams. 12 to 16 with a facilitator and a technical helper, up to 30.
sequence: Learn what each figure on the screen means
Practise spotting changes that matter
A problem is introduced
The team lists possible causes
The team chooses what to do
The figures show the effect
Hand over to a second shift
Review what happened
methods: Digital twin; simulation; team cognition; AAR
mechanics: Attention; transfer-appropriate practice; feedback; contextual interference
setup: Control-room layout with shared dashboards and role stations
needs: A realistic set of data that someone can change during the exercise. In practice this means a spreadsheet or a test system built in advance with the client's own specialists. One person to run the scenario. An observer sheet. Shared screens and technical support.
outputs: Signal library; intervention protocol; handover checklist; team gaps
bestUse: Operations, cyber, product reliability and service management
cautions: Show only the figures the real team uses. If the data and its reactions do not match the real system, people will practise the wrong habits.
plainName: Monitoring and response practice with live data

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome and rules. Then a tour of the screen: what each figure means, what normal looks like and who watches it in real life.
Facilitator, with one of the client's specialists
Shared screens, a one-page key to the figures
Spotting practice. The scenario runner shows six short changes in the figures. Pairs say whether each one matters and why.
Technical helper runs the data. Facilitator takes answers.
Break. Split into two shifts of 6 to 8.
The scenario starts. Shift A takes the role stations. Shift B watches with observer sheets. A problem appears in the figures. Shift A lists possible causes on a board.
Technical helper changes the data. Shift A responds.
Scenario data, role cards, observer sheets, whiteboard
Shift A chooses what to do. The figures change to show the effect. Shift A checks whether it worked and adjusts.
Shift A. Technical helper shows the effect.
Handover. Shift A writes a short note and briefs shift B in 10 minutes. Shift A moves to the observer seats.
Shift B takes over. The problem develops or a second one starts, and one part of it depends on something the handover should have covered.
Technical helper changes the data. Shift B responds.
Scenario data, observer sheets for shift A
Review. Walk through the timeline: when each change appeared, when it was spotted, what was decided, and what the handover left out.
Facilitator, with observers adding what they saw
Timeline from the action log, observer sheets, flipchart
Agree what to keep: the signals to watch for, the steps to take, and a handover checklist. Give each an owner. Close.

name: The Ethical Dilemma Forum
purpose: People work through a hard case with no clear right answer and put their own reasoning into words.
audience: Leaders and professionals. 12 to 16 with one facilitator, up to 50.
sequence: Tell the dilemma as a story
Each person writes their own decision
Map the values that are in tension
Small groups speak for each party affected
Disagree openly, with a facilitator
Test each decision against existing policy and law
Each person writes a revised decision
State the principle behind it
methods: Dilemma case; role-play; fishbowl; structured dialogue
mechanics: Generation; cognitive conflict; perspective-taking; reflection; identity
setup: Circle seating plus stakeholder breakout areas
needs: A facilitator experienced with ethics cases. A case with real tension between two good aims. Ground rules. A named person to go to if the case raises something personal. Chairs in a circle and space for small groups.
outputs: Decision principles; unresolved tensions; policy questions; individual rationale
bestUse: AI ethics, professional standards, inclusion and governance
cautions: Do not write the case as a choice between two options only. Protect people who hold the minority view, and say clearly which parts are legal requirements and which are judgement.
plainName: Ethical dilemma discussion, half day

head: Time
What happens
Who leads
Materials
rows: Welcome. Agree ground rules: speak for yourself, question the reasoning and not the person, and what is said stays in the room. Name the person to go to if the case raises something personal.
Ground rules on a flipchart, chairs in a circle
Tell the dilemma as a story, in two or three parts. Take questions of fact only.
Printed case, handed out after the telling
Each person writes their own decision and their reason. They fold the paper and keep it.
The whole group names the values that pull against each other in the case. Map them on the wall as pairs in tension.
Groups of three or four each take one party affected by the decision. They prepare for 15 minutes, then each group speaks for its party for 3 minutes.
Party cards, space for groups to spread out
Open disagreement, back in the circle. Ask for the least popular view first and make sure it gets a full hearing. Ask people to say what would change their mind.
Test against policy and law. Someone who knows them says which parts of the case are legal requirements and which are judgement. Groups check their decisions against both.
Policy or legal lead, with the facilitator
Relevant policy extracts, one page on the legal position
Each person writes a revised decision and notes what, if anything, changed their thinking.
Each person states the principle behind their decision in one sentence, first to a partner, then round the circle. Record the tensions that remain and any questions for policy owners.
Close. Say what happens to the policy questions. Remind people of the named support person.
